title: Better to know nothing
translation: As a rule, people should know nothing and be good at nothing.

Someone's son, a nice-looking young man, was talking with a guest in front of his father and quoted a line from the Chinese histories. It sounded clever. But with his father sitting there, I thought, he could have done without it.

Another time, at someone's house, we wanted to hear one of the blind priests recite a story to the lute, and sent for a lute. One of its frets had come off. "Make a new one and stick it on," someone said. One of the men there, who seemed decent enough, asked: "Is there an old ladle handle?" I looked at him, and he had grown his nails long. A lute player, then. For a blind priest's lute, none of that mattered. He seemed to want us to see he knew the craft, and it was painful to watch. As someone of rank put it: "Ladle handles are made of what they call bent-wood. It's no good for that."
With young people, the smallest thing makes them look good, or bad.

literal: In general, people should be without knowledge and without ability.
A certain person's son, not bad in appearance and so on, while talking with someone in front of his father, quoted a passage from the histories;
it sounded clever, but I felt that in front of a person to be respected, he need not have.
Also, at a certain person's house, wanting to hear a lute priest's tale, they sent for a lute, and one of its frets had fallen off, so when someone said 'Make one and attach it',
among the men, one who looked not bad said, 'Is there the handle of an old ladle?', and when I looked, he had let his nails grow.
He must play the lute or the like.
A blind priest's lute did not call for such attention.
I wondered if he meant to show he understood the art, and it was painful to watch.
'A ladle handle is what they call bent-wood or some such, and it is no good,' someone (of rank) said.
With young people, even small things make them look good, and make them look bad.

notes.quote: 無智無能なるべきものなり
notes.text: べし: 'should'. Both stories that follow are about showing knowledge at the wrong moment. Section 98 has a similar line: the wise should become fools, the able should become people without ability.
{史書|ししよ}: the Chinese histories, such as the Records of the Grand Historian, part of a young noble's education. {文|もん}: a passage, a quotation.
{尊者|そんじや}: a person to be respected, here his father. {然|さ}らずとも: 'even without doing so', that is, 'he need not have'.
A blind priest reciting a war tale, most likely the Tale of the Heike, to the lute (see section 226).
{柱|ぢう}: a fret on the neck of the lute, as the edition explains; its reading is ぢう. Section 70 has the same word, spelled ぢゆう there. A fret falls off in that section too.
おふす: 'to let grow'. Kenkō concludes from his nails that he plays the lute himself. Commentators explain that some lute techniques were played with the nails instead of the plectrum.
めくら: 'blind'. In Kenkō's time an ordinary word; in modern Japanese it is offensive.
かたはらいたし: 'painful to watch, embarrassing (for someone else)'. き: Kenkō was there.
ひもの: thin cypress board bent into shape, as the edition explains. So the man's idea was not even a good one. {仰|おほ}せられし: someone of high rank, heard by Kenkō himself.
The section ends on a general verdict about young people, after two stories.
